## Overview

The Ho are an Austroasiatic Munda ethnic group of India, concentrated mainly in the Kolhan region of Jharkhand and northern Odisha. They also live in West Bengal, Bihar, Bangladesh and Nepal. In 2001, approximately 700,000 Ho lived in Jharkhand, while the total population in the neighbouring Indian states was 806,921. The Ho language had approximately 1,040,000 speakers according to Ethnologue in 2001; the separate Ho language article gives approximately 2.2 million speakers in India according to the 2001 census. Ho is closely related to Mundari and Santali. Most Ho work in cultivation, while others are agricultural labourers or work in mining. Their folk culture is documented through seasonal festivals, songs, dances, musical instruments, indigenous religious systems and the Warang Chiti writing tradition.

## Material culture

### Architecture

They state that most villages have an *akhra*, a cleared dancing ground of hard earth under a spreading tree.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Copper was smelted in many parts of the old Singhbhum district between the 9th and 12th centuries. Iron ore mining became important in Ho territory, including at Pansira Buru, where the first iron ore mine in India opened in 1901.

## Music & performance

Music is central to Ho festivals and dancing. Ho songs are generally accompanied by dances that change with the seasons, and song and choreographed dance are described as integral parts of Ho culture, art and traditional festivals, especially Mage Parab. Traditional Ho music includes the *Dama*, a drum; the *Dumaṅ*, a barrel drum; and the *Rutu*, a flute. Music and dancing are also part of Sohrai or Gaumára, the village-wide agricultural festival held in honour of cattle used in cultivation. Ho folk literature includes collections of folk songs associated with Sharatchandra Rai, Dr. D.N. Majumdar, B. Sukumar, Haldhaar and Kanhuram Devgum, dated 1915–26. Ho-language broadcasting has also been carried by All India Radio from Keonjhar, Rourkela, Cuttack, Baripada, Chaibasa, Jamshedpur and Ranchi.

## Dance & theatre

Dance is described as more than entertainment for the Ho and as an important part of Adivasi culture. Distinctively choreographed dances accompany seasonal songs and form part of traditional festivals, particularly Mage Parab. Villages commonly have an *akhra*, a cleared dancing ground beneath a spreading tree. Dances are organized on a staggered basis among villages so that other villagers can participate.

## Festivals & rituals

Ho village life revolves around five principal *porob*, or festivals. **Mage Parab** is the most important and takes place in the late winter month of Magha. It marks the completion of the agricultural cycle and lasts one week, honouring Singbonga, the creator god, together with other *bonga*, or spirits. **Baa Porob**, the festival of flowers, is held in mid-spring and celebrates the annual blossoming of sacred Sal trees.

**Sohrai** or **Gaumára** is the principal agricultural festival, usually coinciding with nationwide festivities in the fall. It includes music and dancing in honour of cattle used in cultivation. During the ceremonies, cows are painted with a mixture of flour and dye, anointed with oil and prayed over after a black chicken is sacrificed to an image of the cattle *bonga*.

**Baba Hermúṭu** is the ceremonial first sowing. Its date is set each year in early spring by the *diuri*, or priest, who conducts a three-day ceremony of prayer and first sowing. **Jomnama Porob** takes place in late fall before the first harvest is eaten and gives thanks to the spirits for a trouble-free harvest. Religious rituals are performed by a village priest called a *deuri*, while a spirit doctor called a *deowa* deals with malevolent spirits or deities.

## Foodways

The Ho cultivate crops and have historically lived through settled agriculture. Almost half the population is engaged in cultivation, and another third works as landless agricultural labourers. The sources specifically record that the Ho brew rice wine called *Ḍiaṅ*. The agricultural cycle is ritually marked by Mage Parab, Sohrai or Gaumára, Baba Hermúṭu and Jomnama Porob.

## Oral tradition & literature

Ho folk literature includes folk songs collected by Sharatchandra Rai, Dr. D.N. Majumdar, B. Sukumar, Haldhaar and Kanhuram Devgum in 1915–26. The sources also list Ho works including *Tuturd, Sayan Marsal* by Dr. S.K. Tiyu, *The Affairs of a Tribe* by Dr. D.N. Majumdaar, *Ho Durang* by W.G. Archer and *Folklore of Kolhaan* by C.H. Bompaas. Other listed works include *Ho Lokkatha* by Dr. Aditya Prasad Sinha and literary publications by Ot Guru Kol Lako Bodra, Janum Singh Soy, Balram Paat Pingua and others.

Modern preservation and literary activity include Ho-language magazines such as *Johar*, *Turturd*, *Ottoroad* and *Sarnaphool*, the digital journal *Diyang*, the monthly journal *Dostur Korang*, and Ho-language learning books including *Ol initu* and *Mage Porob*. The first published Ho writing by an ethnic Ho is identified as poetry by Kanuram Deogam in 1930.

## Language & religion

Ho is a Munda language of the Austroasiatic family, closely related to Mundari and Santali and more distantly related to languages including Khmer and Mon. At least three dialects are identified: Lohara, Chaibasa and Thakurmunda; these are mutually intelligible. Ho has been written in Latin, Devanagari and Odia scripts, while the indigenous Warang Chiti alphabet was invented by Lako Bodra in the 20th century. The first published written record dates from 1844 and contains a short word list dated 2 April 1824.

In the 2001 national census, 91% of the Hos of Jharkhand declared that they followed “other religions and persuasions.” Their indigenous religious system is called *Sarna* or Sarnaism, also known as *sarna dhorom*, “religion of the holy woods.” Beliefs in gods, goddesses and spirits are important in everyday life. Singbonga is identified as the creator god, while *bonga* refers to spirits.

commons_photos.title: Documentation of rasi preparation during the production of Mage Porob.jpg
commons_photos.description: Documentation of the preparation of rasi, a mild rice-based alcoholic beverage, for the Ho-language documentation in Keshpada, Mayurbhanj district. Odisha, India. Names of people pictured: Laxmi Haiburu, Subhashish Panigrahi, Kuna Kandeyang, Mathura Deogram, Ladura Singh Haiburu, Bagun Singh. In this picture, Panigrahi is seen capturing a b-roll of Laxmi pouring rasi into a bowl using a phone mounted on a gimbal, and Kandeyang is seen taking a photograph of this process. The photograph was taken from a camera set for capturing a-rolls and is a part of the 2019 documentary film, Mage Porob, directed by Panigrahi.
